M · Final proposal · Formbricks #8650

Check the summary against the code.

The assignment was to make Change Stack’s review screen easier to scan while keeping layers. I focused on one moment: checking a summary, following the access guard, then getting back to the call.

The original already jumps from a summary to code. Here, six points share lines 49–130. I added a separate target for each point and a return path for the guard.

Try the access check →Seven of 52 diffs · manually mapped links · local state only

Compare the same access call

Light · Unified · 1280 × 720

Both captures start at line 54 of access.ts, at commit 23cdac2. The original has more code on screen. M gives file navigation and individual summary links more room.

What differs between these captures?

Same PR, commit, file, starting line, theme, display mode and viewport. These are screenshots of both running interfaces. Their spacing and type sizes remain unchanged, so different amounts of surrounding code fit on screen.

The original shows full summary wording and observed progress. M starts local progress at zero and uses shorter labels, with full wording in a disclosure. M’s submission bar is included. The prototype contains seven added-file diffs; it does not reproduce the original semantic-diff engine.

The original also supports Split. See the earlier source capture. It is supporting context, not the baseline for this comparison.

Try it yourself

Follow the check, then return.

Open the prototype at the access call. Look at what the caller passes to the guard.

  1. Choose Inspect guard in feedback-access.ts. Read the workspace check at line 27 and the entitlement check at line 38.
  2. Choose Return to access.ts. The selected point and reading position should return.
  3. Check that neither file became viewed just by visiting it. Try Mark viewed, then Undo.

Explore beyond that route. The highlight is a place to start checking, not proof that the summary is complete.

Open the working prototype →

Why I kept one code pane

Keeping the caller and guard side by side would squeeze both at laptop width. I chose a return action instead. Persistent files and context also cost code space; Focus gives it back.

I have not tested this with developers. I would ask them to explain the access check on both screens, then find something the summary misses. If precise links make them overlook surrounding code, I would change the approach.
